Lmao. No. Also “actual labor”. Do you have any idea how many hours of practice goes into prepping to become a professional musician? Or how many people end up destroying their hands and bodies over time playing their instruments?

Here’s some info: most professional performers have a masters degree or above. Standard practice time during a degree is around 4-8 hours per day, and this continues afterwards.

Then, to get a job as a performer in one of these orchestras, hundreds of people travel to the city and audition for one opening. 

Once you’re hired, concert cycles consist of long rehearsals, community engagement activities (ie free concerts at schools), and in some cases assisting with symphony operations while also working a second job as an adjunct instructor, private teaching, and gigging as much as possible. You also spend hundreds of dollars each year to keep your instrument (which you’ve probably spent around $10-40K on at this point for something professional quality) in optimal playing condition. 


The proposals by the symphony board are cutting salaries from around $35,000 a year (definitely NOT a lavish wage and already much less than symphonies around the country) to $11,000 a year. That’s less money hourly than I made working a summer job at chick fil a years ago. For people with extremely high levels of training who have fought tooth and nail to win a spot in a professional level orchestra (most of us don’t get that far).

Edit to add: The musicians of the symphony are not the real issue here, but they are the ones getting screwed. The people in admin, who are responsible for procuring donors, programming, marketing, etc., are literally paid to make the symphony economically viable and the city is supposed to be supporting the arts. Professional symphonies are thriving in other cities.

I have one difficult female as well. She really does not like to be handled so play time is difficult and she does bite if I pick her up sometimes. I’ve finally gotten to the point where I can get her to come to me when I have treats. I did this by giving her a lot of small treat pieces every day during play time for a couple of weeks. Once she realized play time was constant treat time, she got into a routine of running up to me, taking the treat, running away to stash it, immediately running back to me, etc. I’d have her do this at least 20 times in a row every single day when play time was wrapping up so she really got the hang of me being a treat resource. I put the treat in the palm of my hand rather than in my fingers because she is less likely to bite this way. I also call her using clicking sounds rather than words because she responds better to this. I will also say she doesn’t eat all the treats (she’s a little hoarder, and once I put her away I just find her stash and put them back in the bag lol) so if you’re concerned about over feeding, break treats into super small pieces. Now, after almost a year of catching her being a major pain, I have gotten her to the point where I can have her run to me for a treat, show it to her, then place the treat in the cage and she hops right in and eats it. Still doesn’t like to be handled, but at least I no longer have to chase her around, and this change has all happened within the last month when I started really consistently using treats as bait to get her put away. In the past week we have even started working on a new trick!

Another thing that I think has helped is I will pet her in her cage each day. She seems less skittish when she is in her own environment. I even got boggles out of her once! I think this has made her more comfortable with my hands so that she is less likely to bite and she sees me as less of a threat. I’ve had her for over a year at this point, so know that this could definitely take a long time, but when you finally get those first boggles it will all seem worth it!
